summary:
An opinion piece by Marian Salzman (SVP, Corporate Development, PMI U.S.) and Dr. Kaleen Love (Chief People and Culture Officer, PMI U.S.) arguing that the traditional bridge between higher education and employment is breaking down. Students apply to hundreds of jobs without response while employers claim they cannot find talent; career services offices and hiring managers are both overwhelmed, and generative AI is worsening the strain.

The authors frame the core problem not as a skills gap but a translation gap: students are trained to accumulate credentials but not to articulate who they are, how they think, or why they matter. Employers say they want curiosity, resilience, adaptability, ethical judgment, emotional intelligence and communication, yet applicant-tracking systems screen for keywords and filter those qualities out before any human conversation. Students can generate a resume with AI in seconds, and some use AI to supply live interview answers, but many have not learned handshakes, eye contact, ambiguity, or telling their own story unmediated.

Blame is shared. Universities treated career services as an administrative afterthought and behave as though the degree is the finished product rather than a launchpad. This disadvantages first-generation students, veterans, community college graduates and nontraditional learners, who lack the inherited fluency in networking language and workplace etiquette that higher-income, white-collar families pass along. Employers, during and after COVID, dismantled relationship-driven campus recruiting and replaced experienced recruiters with portals, algorithms and efficiency metrics.

PMI U.S. has convened roundtables with career services representatives and reports that the strongest-outcome institutions embed experiential learning and teach professional communication, networking, ethical AI use and adaptive thinking as career skills rather than soft skills. The authors argue technical skills have short shelf lives and that synthesis, judgment, trust-building, leadership and human connection will define the next 20 years. PMI U.S. cites its 10-week paid summer internships for rising seniors aged 21+ and a Senior Fellow leadership program, screening for creative thinking, motivation, tenacity and purpose over GPA.
